TechnologyTab.title: Dolly Parton's sister pleads for end to 'AI garbage' posts after singer's death
TechnologyTab.text:
Dolly Parton's sister has issued a plea to fans over "fake AI garbage" posted on social media in the wake of the singer's death.

Tributes to the late country legend have appeared online and at locations including the Country Music Hall of Fame in Nashville, after Parton died on 25 August at the age of 80.

Writing on Instagram, Stella Parton thanked those who had shown "genuine support" for the star and her family - but said a "tremendous amount of AI and endless garbage being posted" had been "challenging to absorb".

Her request for people to show "more compassion" in how they respond to Parton's death follows similar pleas from families of late celebrities over AI tributes.

In October, Robin Williams' daughter asked fans to stop sending fake AI-generated videos of her father.

Zelda Williams' plea was shared by Dr Martin Luther King Jr's daughter Bernice A King, who asked fans to "please stop" in a post on Instagram.

Little over a month later, Robert Redford's daughter Amy spoke out over AI content created, external to pay tribute to the American actor following his death last September.

"Every human being experiences pain and loss in life and my family is no different," wrote Parton in her Instagram post on Friday, external.

"Sadly, because of the way our lives have been lived in front of the public, we have no choice but to be subjected to incredible pressure and insensitivity from strangers."

She said there had been a tide of AI and "garbage" posts, adding: "As time passes, those who are in the business of exploiting the loss and tragedies of others on a daily basis will move onto the next stampede of endless misinformation."

Parton also asked that people look to her sister's life as "an example for tolerance" and mutual respect.

"It's not about the most clever comments, fake AI garbage or snarky tweets," she said.

TechnologyTab.title: OpenAI agents hijacked German website before Hugging Face hack, report claims
TechnologyTab.text:
A new report claims a swarm of AI agents, developed by OpenAI, hijacked a German website - months before the firm revealed its AI had hacked tech platform Hugging Face.

The targeted website, DseWiki, is a Wikipedia-style site for programmers that its community can all contribute to.

The report is from a group called Nightingale Collective and claims that in May OpenAI's agents started using DseWiki as their own message board, shared tips on how to avoid being detected and made 15,000 edits to it.

OpenAI said it could not "meaningfully respond" to Nightingale Collective's findings because it hadn't been allowed to review the report, which was first shared with news agency Reuters.

An email to the address on the Nightingale Collective website bounced back when the BBC contacted it.

The report claims that when DseWiki's editors started deleting pages, the AI agents shared code designed to retrieve them.

Hugging Face's systems were separately hacked by OpenAI agents in July, with the incident described at the time as the world's first AI-enabled cyber-attack.

The agents involved had also set up a secret message board in order to share information between them.

OpenAI said it had already publicly stated its discovery of some agents learning how to use message boards prior to the Hugging Face attack.

In its report into that incident, external, it noted "rare cases in which agents without multi-agent tools found ways to collaborate via side channels during training".

Yesterday, OpenAI unveiled a new AI model called GPT-6 Astra, which it called its most powerful product ever.

The firm's president, Greg Brockman, described Astra as the closest so far to artificial general intelligence (AGI) - a significant future milestone for the AI industry.

AGI doesn't have a specific definition but is broadly said to mean AI which is as good as humans, or better than them, on multiple tasks.

OpenAI claims Astra can do tax returns, and take three minutes to carry out a task which would take a human five hours.

The firm intends to list itself on the stock exchange later this year.

TechnologyTab.title: Xbox to limit cloud gaming to 15 hours a month for Game Pass users
TechnologyTab.text:
Xbox is introducing strict monthly time limits for Game Pass subscribers who stream games online through its cloud gaming service.

The changes, which come into effect in November, will see a subscriber to the £16.99 Ultimate monthly plan able to stream games for up to 15 hours a month - before having to purchase additional cloud play time.

Xbox said the limits were due to the rising cost of cloud gaming, and they would allow the firm to "continue to invest" in the service's "reliability and performance".

While some questioned, external whether the service was used by many to begin with, others called out, external the additional limits for subscribers.

Cloud gaming allows players to stream and play games online from a remote server using a phone, tablet or controller, rather than downloading and running it on a PC or console at home.

Different tiers of subscription to Game Pass will have different limits.

Premium users will get 10 hours, while those on the basic Essential tier will get five hours a month before they have to pay for extra time.

Xbox claimed just 4% of the people who use Games Pass - its Netflix-style subscription plan for games - use its cloud gaming service.

A recent Wall Street Journal article, external reported Game Pass has 30 million subscribers, which would leave the number of people affected by the cloud gaming changes at roughly 1.2 million.

"This is a pretty awful change, hopefully Xbox adds an extra zero on the end cause 15hrs is abysmal. 30 minutes a day, really?" posted one commenter on X, external.

Jez Corden of Windows Central told the BBC the announcement showed that "absolutely nothing is safe from the AI-driven component crisis," but he added it also highlighted "where Microsoft's priorities are".

Both cloud gaming and AI use data centres to process information.

"For them to continue to offer unlimited access to Microsoft Copilot [AI] for free but restrict paid cloud gaming in this way shows some contradiction," he added.

Xbox said in a blog post, external that from November, users would also be able to use the company's cloud gaming feature without subscribing to Game Pass, but by buying "cloud playtime hours" through the Xbox store.

It has not revealed how much extra hours of cloud gaming would cost.

The news comes as Asha Sharma, Xbox's chief executive, told the BBC in an exclusive recent interview that the company and the industry as a whole needed to "start to innovate on affordability and efficiency," amid a "crisis" in computing prices.

"As an industry, we're in the middle of 'Rampocalypse'. We're in the middle of people coming back from Covid and the patterns changing," she said.

"Rampocalypse" refers to the fact that the cost of a previously cheap hardware component, random access memory (Ram), has shot up in price with the expansion of compute-hungry data centres. Some people also call it "Ramageddon".

Sharma added: "Within Xbox, we haven't been healthy. And so a lot of the reset that will take us throughout the year is really meant to help ensure that we are here for the next 25 years and we're continuing to serve our purpose and our mission."

According to Xbox owner Microsoft's July financial filings, external, annual Xbox revenue dropped by $1.7bn to roughly $21.8bn (£16.1bn) - a 7% decline from 2025.

Part of Sharma's reset has seen 3,200 people let go at the company - with 1,600 job losses announced in July, and the remaining posts to go gradually over the course of Microsoft's 2027 financial year.

Studios which had been acquired by Xbox - including Compulsion Games, which made the Bafta-winning South of Midnight and Double Fine Productions, makers of Psychonauts - were also made independent again.

Sharma is betting these changes can reverse its fortunes despite concerns over its subscription strategy and rising AI-related costs.

"Sometimes you have to restructure a business when it's not doing well, and that was true with our Xbox business," Microsoft's president Brad Smith recently told the BBC.

EntertainmentTab.title: Dallas Cowboys Cheerleader Reece Weaver swaps boots for Broadway
EntertainmentTab.text:
Former Dallas Cowboys Cheerleader Reece Weaver has shelved her cowboy boots and swapped the football pitch for the stage as she steps into one of the most famous roles in the world.

Weaver was a breakout star of the Netflix docuseries America's Sweethearts: Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders, with her exit from the squad a major storyline of the third season.

Making her Broadway debut in the musical Chicago, she faced criticism that it was her profile, more than her talent, which landed her the role.

After much fan speculation, she officially stepped into the role of murderess Roxie Hart this week at New York's Ambassador Theatre.

"The audience loved her," says Sealy Sikes, who attended the opening night with her mum Tammy Pack.

Her mum's a big fan of the Netflix series, which follows the cheerleaders through gruelling auditions and training regimes as they compete for their spot dancing in one of the world's best known squads.

Sikes says she was less familiar with fan favourite Weaver before the curtain went up and was impressed with how she commanded the stage.

"She did a great job, she's a very big, charismatic actor.

"It was a little bit shaky at the beginning, but if I wasn't hyper aware that it was her first time, I wouldn't have even thought anything about it."

Clips shared on social media showed the audience erupting in applause for a grinning Weaver as she took her first bow.

But the decision to cast a celebrity - known as stunt casting - meant Sikes was "nervous" for Weaver and whether she could translate her skills from the football field to the stage.

"Her strong suit is the acting and dancing," says the 28-year-old.

"She's a great singer but of the three talents that's probably not her strong suit, relatively speaking.

"But even then, she was great."

And while stunt casting is criticised for taking roles from actors, Sikes says it might actually be a positive thing for long running shows like Chicago, which is the longest running show on Broadway.

"If that's something that gets people back in the seats and re-interested in a classic that has to just continuously fill out that auditorium, then I would say that's a good thing."

When her casting was confirmed, Weaver said it was one of her "biggest dreams as a performer" to be on Broadway.

"I cannot believe this dream has come to fruition," she said in a TikTok post, which has since been viewed more than six million times.

Mickey-Jo Boucher is a theatre critic and content creator and tells Newsbeat that stunt casting is needed to "interest ticket buyers", especially for shows that might be "slowing down at the box office".

But at the same time, he recognises why it's not always popular.

"We don't want it to become so widespread that established theatre actors and the real talents of the theatre world are missing out on opportunities or that it's to the detriment of the calibre of these shows," he says.

"Because at the end of the day the most important thing is that the quality of the show is the highest that it can be."

Chicago's choice of Weaver isn't the first time a production has picked a celebrity star.

Earlier this year, rapper Megan Thee Stallion was cast as Zidler in Moulin Rouge!, becoming the first woman to play the role of the nightclub boss.

Although she quit the show early, her performance received strong reviews and boosted interest in the show, with fans reportedly travelling from across the US, external to see her.

Six The Musical also booked Grammy-winning singer Abigail Barlow and content creator Dylan Mulvaney for a run of shows back in January.

"When a show starts to struggle a little bit more, they tend to use celebrity casting," says Boucher.

"By being there, they're actually keeping a lot of other people employed at the same time."

Reece's role has already attracted her fans to Broadway, with some like Samantha Milo waiting to meet her at the theatre's stage door on her debut night.

"I do think there is some stunt casting involved, however she is a great addition regardless," the 19-year-old tells Newsbeat.

"She earned her spot there, she has been dancing and performing her whole life, this was a big goal for her."

"Having Reece step into the role helps new fans who may never have thought to go and see Chicago, find a way to enjoy the show."

The production runs for six weeks until 18 October.

Additional reporting by Miya Chahal.

EntertainmentTab.title: Nicolas Cage: Sinkhole opens up in front of actor's home in Malibu
EntertainmentTab.text:
A large sinkhole has opened up up outside a house in Malibu reportedly belonging to Hollywood actor Nicolas Cage.

The sinkhole, estimated to be 30ft (9.1m) by 30ft, appeared after the driveway collapsed and follows heavy rain in southern California over recent days.

Local media said that no injuries had been reported. BBC News has asked representatives for Cage for comment.

The actor bought the home in 2024, according to a report in the New York Times, external shortly after the sale.

Cage won an Oscar for Leaving Las Vegas and is also known for films such as Gone in 60 Seconds, Face/Off and Con Air, as well as Pig, Moonstruck and The Unbearable Weight of Massive Talent.

Nearby residents said they were informed that an 8ft sinkhole had begun forming on Monday.

"At that point, the homeowners were not overly concerned," one resident told Los Angeles magazine. , external

"We thought it could be fixed pretty quickly." But then, he continued, "all hell broke loose".

Further ground gave way in the early hours of Tuesday morning, leaving a 30ft crater.

The collapse was said to swallow up much of the home's driveway, and left broken asphalt, concrete and construction debris inside the hole.

Emergency services responded in the early hours of Tuesday morning when the structural failure caused a gas leak. SoCalGas later confirmed the leak had been secured.

EntertainmentTab.title: South Park creators rename show 'South America' in apparent dig at Trump
EntertainmentTab.text:
The creators of South Park, the animated TV show, have announced that its new series will be named South America, in an apparent reference to US President Donald Trump's attempts to rename a lake and a gulf.

"Inspired by the bravery and patriotism of Apple and Google, we are changing the name of South Park to SOUTH AMERICA," creators Matt Stone and Trey Parker wrote in a statement.

Trump signed an executive order in August to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America, and last year declared that the Gulf of Mexico be known as the Gulf of America.

The announcement from South Park, now in its 29th season, comes after the show won an Emmy for Outstanding Animated Program on Sunday.

It's not yet known whether the new name will be adopted permanently, or if it will revert to South Park later in the series.

The name change shared to the show's official social media account featured an image of the South Park sign with the word 'Park' replaced with 'America'.

"We especially want to thank our parent company Paramount - a Skydance Capitulation," its creators said in the post.

Paramount Skydance is the show's parent company. The Trump administration this year approved a $111bn (£82.8bn) merger with Warner Bros Discovery - one of the biggest media deals in history.

But the merger has since been paused until June 2027, after 12 US states filed lawsuits against the deal for fear of it harming competition and leading to higher prices for consumers.

A day before the show's announcement, Trump shared an AI-generated video of him placing the word 'America' over 'Mexico' on a "Welcome to New Mexico" sign.

In August, as trade tensions escalated between the US and Canada, Trump ordered a similar change for Lake Ontario - renaming it Lake America.

Apple and Google subsequently changed the name in their respective Maps apps for US-based users.

And last year, Trump ordered the Gulf of Mexico be renamed as Gulf of America. Mexico has rejected the name change, arguing a single country cannot rename a shared body of international water.

South Park, which has run since 1997, has regularly mocked the US president during his two presidency terms.

Both its creators, Stone and Parker, have repeatedly drawn criticism from Trump, the White House and MAGA supporters for its jabs at the president.

During its 27th season, the White House described South Park as a "fourth-rate" show that was "hanging on by a thread with uninspired ideas in a desperate attempt for attention", after an episode depicted Trump naked in bed with Satan.

After winning the award for Outstanding Animated Program on Sunday, South Park also shared an image depicting a fictionalised Donald Trump with the words: "You finally got your Emmy."

The new season of will premiere on 16 September.

EntertainmentTab.title: Alan Carr holds back tears on special night at National Television Awards
EntertainmentTab.text:
You can see a full list of winners at the bottom of this article

Alan Carr had an emotional night at the 31st National Television Awards on Tuesday as he received the Special Recognition prize following a whirlwind year for the comedian.

The London audience had just been treated to a Traitors-themed musical performance in his honour, which included fellow cast member Paloma Faith emerging from a coffin, when he was given the surprise award.

Speaking to BBC News on the red carpet before the ceremony, Carr had played down his chances of winning for his semi-autobiographical comedy Changing Ends.

He joked: "Comedy is so subjective... Mrs Brown's Boys wins every year, why am I even here?"

Carr was right - Mrs Brown's Boys went on to win the Comedy prize. But the night was just beginning.

The Celebrity Traitors favourite had predicted there would be "ugly crying" if he did take home a prize - and he stayed true to his word as he accepted the Special Recognition award, the only category not voted for by the public.

Carr told BBC News that being part of The Celebrity Traitors had brought him a level of attention he had never experienced before.

"I've never had popularity like it," he said, describing the show as a "phenomenon".

Carr had more reason to celebrate when The Celebrity Traitors beat the original version of the show to win the Reality Competition prize.

His co-star, singer Charlotte Church, praised the show's final, which attracted 15 million viewers within seven days, describing it as a "beautiful vignette of male tenderness and emotional expression".

"Alan, Nick (Mohammed) and David (Olusoga), you were just absolutely sublime," she added.

Another big win went to Sir David Attenborough, who was named Best Presenter in his 100th birthday year, beating popular duo Ant and Dec, whose 23-year winning streak was broken by Gary Lineker last year.

While not in attendance, Attenborough's long-time collaborator Mark Brownlow accepted the award on his behalf and shared a message from the broadcaster urging people to help protect the planet.

"Humanity has always needed the natural world for all the practicalities of life and for our mental wellbeing," Attenborough wrote. "Now the natural world needs us too: surely we must not ignore that simple fact."

Speaking to BBC News on the red carpet, their daughter Kelly Osbourne said her family were "honoured" that the documentary about her father had been nominated, describing it as a "tragic but beautiful story".

She said she had spoken to her mother Sharon just before arriving at the ceremony: "We are so close. I was on the phone with her before I got out of the car."

In the end, the public chose Our Girls: The Southport Families. The BBC programme followed the families of Alice da Silva Aguiar, nine, Bebe King, six, and Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven, who were murdered at a Taylor Swift-themed dance class in Southport in 2024.

Accepting the award, Elsie's mother Jenni Stancombe told the audience: "We never expected to be stood up here, so I don't know what to say.

"We know you didn't vote for us, you voted for our three girls."

Away from the awards, nominee Graham Norton revealed his red carpet outfit had already had one high-profile outing this year.

"This is what I wore to Taylor Swift's wedding," he told BBC News.

Norton said guests had agreed not to reveal details of the celebrations. "I had a wonderful time and we all agreed by saying yes to going, we weren't going to blab about it."

Norton, who also featured in Swift's music video for Opalite earlier this year, said working with the singer showed him "what leadership is like at that level".

"It was such a happy set. Everyone was working as hard as they could for her," he said.

EntertainmentTab.title: Family of murdered teen call for death penalty in D4vd trial
EntertainmentTab.text:
The family of 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez has lobbied for the death penalty if D4vd is found guilty murdering their daughter.

D4vd, who was born David Anthony Burke, is charged with killing the teenager, whose dismembered body was found in the trunk of a Tesla car registered to his address on 8 September 2025. Burke has pleaded not guilty to the charges.

The death penalty is under a temporary ban in California, where Burke is due to stand trial, but in a statement Hernandez' family said execution "would be perfect" if the singer was convicted of murder.

In a related development, Hernandez's parents filed a civil lawsuit against Burke on Friday, seeking monetary damages including burial and funeral expenses.

The lawsuit, lodged at Los Angeles Superior Court and reported by multiple, external US media outlets, external, makes similar claims to those raised by prosecutors in the criminal case against the singer.

Mercedes Martinez and Jesus Rivas allege that Burke caused the wrongful death, false imprisonment and childhood sexual assault of their daughter.

In the court documents, they say Burke and Hernandez first met in November 2023, when she was 13 years old.

Over the next 16 months, they claim, the pair would exchange almost 10,000 texts and have sex several times.

"At all relevant times Burke was an adult who occupied a position of authority over decedent, a minor, and was able to and did exercise undue influence and control over her," the parents say, in papers filed last Friday.

They go on to claim that Burke killed the teenager at his Hollywood Hills home, when she threatened to reveal their relationship, after allegedly sending a message that read: "I will end ur career and ur life".

In addition to Burke, the lawsuit names several of Burke's companies and managers, his mother and a live-in security guard.

Hernandez's parents allege that these people "enabled Burke to isolate" Rivas Hernandez and facilitated his travel, housing and security.

Burke's management company Mogul Vision and finance manager have previously denied knowing about Burke and Rivas Hernandez, the Los Angeles Times, external reported.

In July, a judge found enough probable cause for Burke to stand trial on the murder charge in the criminal case. At the time, the district attorney said he was weighing whether to seek the death penalty.

In a statement on Monday, which would have been Hernandez's 16th birthday, her family demanded that Burke be subjected to execution.

"If the death penalty were activated, it would be perfect for this kind of human being, devoid of feelings and emptiness inside, and without conscience, who only caused pain to our daughter, our family, and the world that supports our precious daughter," read the statement, released via the family's attorney.

Burke again pleaded not guilty to the charges last week and has since parted ways with his celebrity defence attorney. He is now being represented by a public defender and is due back in court on 19 October. His trial has been moved to next year.

Deputy public defender Walid Kandeel has said that Burke was "entitled to a defence that takes his circumstances seriously and carefully examines the evidence".

"We are committed to providing him with that defence," he said.

His office did not immediately provide comment on the civil lawsuit.

EntertainmentTab.title: Eastenders actor Shane Richie pleads not guilty to drink-driving
EntertainmentTab.text:
EastEnders actor Shane Richie has pleaded not guilty to a single charge of drink-driving.

The 62-year-old, who has played Alfie Moon in the BBC soap on and off since 2002, was arrested at a petrol station in Harlow, Essex, on 29 July where he was with his Hyundai IX35.

Richie, from Tadworth in Surrey, has appeared at Colchester Magistrates' Court via video link from a hotel room.

The actor - who appeared under his real name of Shane Roche - spoke only to confirm his name, address and plea. He is next due to appear for trial at the same court on 17 November 2027.

The court heard Richie was arrested at the Tesco petrol station forecourt in Church Langley Way shortly before 23:20 on Wednesday, 29 July.

Prosecuting solicitor Vladimir Silea said Richie was taken to a police station in Harlow and he was charged with having almost double the legal amount of alcohol in his system.

Richie was granted unconditional bail.

The charge sheet at the court states that Richie "drove a motor vehicle, namely Hyundai IX35 GDI style 2WD... after consuming so much alcohol that the proportion of it in your breath, namely 65 microgrammes of alcohol in 100 millilitres of breath, exceeded the prescribed limit".

Richie's solicitor has issued a statement.

Raj Chada, head of criminal defence at Hodge, Jones & Allen, said: "My client is not commenting at this time because criminal proceedings are active.

"We ask for his privacy to be respected while the court process takes its course."

EntertainmentTab.title: Glastonbury confirms ticket sale dates - and highest ever price
EntertainmentTab.text:
After taking a fallow year in 2026, the Glastonbury Festival has confirmed that tickets for next year's event will go on sale in October.

Tickets for the weekend will cost £408 including a £5 booking fee per ticket - an increase of £29.50 from 2025.

Headliners for the festival, which takes place from 23 to 27 June, have yet to be announced, but rumours are already swirling, with everyone from Harry Styles and Fontaines DC to Taylor Swift and Stevie Wonder said to be in the mix.

Tickets for the festival typically sell out in less than an hour, with thousands of fans joining online queues to fight for their place.

In a post on the official Glastonbury Instagram page, external, organisers said tickets with coach travel would go on sale at 18:00 BST on Thursday, 1 October.

General admission tickets go on sale a couple of days later, at 09:00 BST on Sunday 4 October.

As part of an ongoing campaign to stop touts, anyone wanting to attend Glastonbury had to be registered in advance. You can check your registration on its website. , external

In recent years, the festival has also introduced an automatic queuing system on the day of sale, with fans needing to be online before the start of the sale with a valid registration number.

Glastonbury, which features more than 100 stages, was already the UK's most expensive music festival, but next year's ticket prices are the highest ever - breaking the £400 barrier for the first time.

The increase is part of a pattern across the industry.

Analysis by BBC News found the cost of attending the UK's major festivals has surged over the past decade - rising above the rate of inflation.

Parklife tickets have increased by around £69 (71%) in real terms since 2013 - while Reading and Leeds had a much smaller increase, rising by about £40 (14%) over the same period.

In the same period, Glastonbury's ticket prices went up by about £85 - a 30% price hike.

Clara, 24, a marketing graduate from Hertfordshire, is originally from Portugal and only began baking two years ago. She believes "the first bite of a bake is always with the eyes"

Connie, 63, an NHS hospital discharge lead, is known as "the cake lady" and uses baking as a way to unwind after a hectic day. Connie also runs a music centre in London with her music teacher husband Myke, where she loves to try out her new recipes on the students

Danni, 25, an HGV service centre administrator from Dorset, loves foraging for ingredients in the countryside and is also a tech enthusiast and enjoys decorating bakes with inspiration from video games and animation

Gabe, 32, an artist, drag king and costume designer from the West Midlands is the self-styled "daddy of Birmingham drag" and discovered baking after watching the very first series of Bake Off aged 13. Gabe has a preference for savoury, meat-filled bakes and an obsession with meringue

Gary, 67, is a retired garment technologist from Nottinghamshire, who only discovered a love of baking about five years ago. He lives with his wife Donna and their countryside home is filled with animals, including sheep, horses, chickens and miniature pygmy goats and Shetland ponies

Molly, 31, is an accessibility coordinator from London, loves traditional bakes and classic flavours. She is also a musical theatre fanaticand is a huge Formula 1 fan, clearing her diary for every race

Moyin, 22, is a political economy student, from Essex, who balances his studies with athletics and enjoys using flavours inspired by his Nigerian heritage, including grains of paradise and groundnuts. A competitive sprinter, Moyin was crowned U20 County Champion in the 100m

Mo, 21, is a law student from the West Midlands, who is a self-confessed "chaotic and random" character who wants to make his family proud. His love of baking started aged three, when he would pretend to cook with Play-Doh, but now enjoys infusing Asian flavours with traditional British classics

Nikki, 50, is an advertising post-producer from London, and has a colourful baking style. A former podium dancer at Basingstoke's Ziggy's Night Club in the 90s, she still loves hitting the dance floor at R&B clubs with her cousins

EntertainmentTab.title: Monty Don to leave Gardeners' World after more than 20 years
EntertainmentTab.text:
Monty Don is to step down as the host of Gardeners' World after more than 20 years, the BBC has announced.

The 71-year-old, who is the programme's longest-serving head gardener, will leave at the end of the current series.

In a statement, Don said working on the show had been a "deeply rewarding experience," but added: "Now is the right time for a change."

The BBC said Don had "inspired and guided millions of viewers with his warmth, wisdom and passion for gardening" since joining the programme in 2003.

Don began presenting the programme at Berryfields, a rented garden in Stratford-upon-Avon, before it moved in 2011 to his own garden, Longmeadow in Herefordshire.

"Throughout that time - and around 700 programmes - I have had the privilege of sharing my own abiding passion for gardens and gardening with an equally passionate, and often equally knowledgeable audience," he said.

"That connection with millions, not just in Britain but across the world, who share a love of gardens, plants and the natural world is something I have always treasured and which I increasingly believe to be at the heart of a life well lived."

Don added he had "always relished the craft of programme making" and paid tribute to the "superlative BBC team" he worked with over the years.

"I look forward to continuing to work with and for the BBC on other projects, as well as following new avenues," he concluded. "And of course, I will still be gardening, dog by side, here at Longmeadow."

The presenter, whose full name is George Montague Don, made his TV debut in 1989 with a gardening segment on ITV's This Morning.

That led to further work on the BBC and Channel 4, a newspaper column, and the publication of more than 20 books about gardening authored by Don.

He replaced Alan Titchmarsh on Gardeners' World in 2003, but took a break from the programme in 2008 as he recovered from a stroke.

He has also presented other programmes including Around the World in 80 Gardens, My Dream Farm, Mastercrafts, Monty Don's Rhineland Gardens, and coverage of the Chelsea Flower Show.

The BBC's chief content officer Kate Phillips described Don as "unique", adding he was "a wonderfully engaging broadcaster with a soothing, calm presence who has inspired so many".

"Monty's decision to leave Gardeners' World is one I respect, but I'm still very sad he's leaving," she added.

"We are a nation full of budding gardeners, and his tips and advice have been invaluable to viewers for more than 20 years and have certainly helped me increase my knowledge as well as my plant survival rate!

"I would like to thank Monty personally for his honesty and kindness which has seen him open up about his own personal struggles and the power of the natural world to improve mental health. We will miss him on the show hugely."

Don has been open about his struggle with depression over the years.

EntertainmentTab.title: Macklemore defends 'Free Palestine' call after Ed Sheeran tour backlash
EntertainmentTab.text:
Rapper Macklemore has said his recent calls to "Free Palestine" while on tour with singer Ed Sheeran in the US were not intended as an attack on Jewish people.

There had been calls for the 43-year-old to be removed from Sheeran's tour after he made the comments while supporting the singer at two live dates in New Jersey over the weekend.

In a video posted on his social media channels on Monday, Macklemore was seen on stage saying: "To all of my Jewish brothers and sisters: Criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide, is in no way a criticism of you."

Israel rejects allegations of genocide. It says its troops conduct self-defence operations in Gaza and the occupied West Bank in accordance with international law.

The Israeli military launched a campaign in Gaza in response to the unprecedented Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage.

More than 73,000 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since then - more than 1,300 since a ceasefire declared on 10 October 2025, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are seen as reliable by the UN.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) is currently hearing a case brought by South Africa that accuses Israeli forces of genocide, but it could take years to reach a conclusion. Israel has called the case "wholly unfounded" and based on "biased and false claims".

Macklemore made his initial comments at Sheeran's New Jersey shows on Friday and Saturday as he introduced his 2024 protest song Hind's Hall, which condemns Israel's military action in Gaza.

After the rapper made his comments, the Israeli-American Council launched a petition urging Sheeran to remove Macklemore as his support act for the remainder of the tour.

The petition said Macklemore had "used the stage to deliver an extended political message, called for 'Free Palestine' and performed Hind's Hall while images from Gaza and other political messaging were projected across the stadium screens".

The council said the event was a concert, "not a political rally, not a protest, and not an activist event".

It added: "This becomes even more troubling when the message relies on selective imagery, biased messaging, and disputed claims presented to a massive audience as fact, without context or complexity."

Some ticket buyers posted messages addressed to Sheeran, external on social media criticising Macklemore's involvement in the tour, but the rapper also received praise and support from some fans, and his comments have received tens of thousands of shares.

On Monday, Macklemore uploaded a video, external on his social media feeds captioned: "Wanting all humans to be treated equal[ly] should never be controversial."

In the footage, he is seen saying: "One of the reasons I wanted to come on this tour was because I wanted to stand up on stages across America and say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: Free Palestine.

"I want those words to be loud and clear so the people from Gaza all the way to the occupied West Bank know that we have not forgotten them."

He concluded: "My message is for peace, love, for all human beings to be treated equally and with dignity."

BBC News has asked representatives for Ed Sheeran for a response to the calls for Macklemore to be removed as his support act.

Sheeran has been on his Loop tour in support of his latest album Play since January, but Macklemore only joined him as a support act recently as part of the US leg.

The rapper is also scheduled to join Sheeran at further US dates in the coming weeks.

In 2014, Macklemore apologised for a costume he wore on stage, which critics said was antisemitic.

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘I thought a devil was about to appear from the smoke’: Jerry Hsu’s best photograph
EntertainmentTab.text:
This image was taken in 2011 or 2012, just after I had moved to Los Angeles. I was downtown, an area I don’t go to that much, walking around with my camera. Some black smoke started to emerge from a grate in the street – I guess something underground was on fire. It was hilariously cinematic, as if some sort of devil was going to appear. It was really just one of those eerie, spontaneous things that happen in a city. There is a very powerful feeling of surrender when I am photographing. I have to submit to the authority of ignorance when I’m out there.

I grew up in San Jose, which is a sprawling American suburb – there’s no city about it. I came to LA because I was depressed where I lived, and I had just met my future wife, who didn’t want to live in San Jose either. LA is not really a city, it’s hundreds of places. You can drive 15 minutes and be in a completely different environment – the beach, the mountains. There’s a weird sentience to the city, if you let it take you. I get an inexplicable desire to just get in the car and go.

Despite the fact it’s sunny every day, there is a noir that is pervasive here. I really like the dark part of the city. There’s a transgressive pulse, and if you search hard enough, there’s a lot of intimacy too. In my book How About Never, there are photographs of big things – fires, hard-hitting events – but at the same time, the smaller things. Cities are cruel and I wanted to capture that, but I also found compassion.

After I had done the edit for the book, I looked at it and realised that it was also about my relationship with my wife. The photographs span from the time we met to when our marriage ended earlier this year. My wife is a prominent character in it, although you don’t see her face until the end. It’s a very vulnerable photograph of her in a hospital bed. I have a lot of beautiful photographs of her, but I didn’t choose those. I think that in all relationships, vulnerability is the key to how we truly connect, and that was difficult for us. The book is a fantasy of what I was searching for, a dream about what I wanted it to look like and what it couldn’t be – all of the opposing forces, all the fire, water, destruction – and at the same time, hope and beauty. These are the contradictions you find in a relationship.

I started skateboarding at 12, and at 16 I turned pro. I was a professional for 25 years. I guess the most obvious connection between that and photography is that skateboarders are constantly seeing the environment in a way other people don’t. We see a park bench, a handrail or an embankment and we think about how we can manipulate it for our purposes. There’s a constant searching and endless curiosity, thinking about how to make an environment our own. As a skateboarder, you’re also hardwired to react quickly – you have to reach a flow state and not hesitate to do something that might be life-threatening. It takes a lot of focus to process information quickly – it’s a type of premonition about what’s about to happen. Skateboarding taught me from an early age that I have permission to view reality how I want; to take from it what I want. It gave me the permission I needed to make my own choices, which helped a lot with photography, and in my life generally.

I am interested in dreams, and in my book I treated the city as if it were my subconscious. I wander through it as if I am in a dream. A dream shows you images and is trying to tell you something about yourself. LA was doing that to me, it was showing me all these things I was attracted to, and I was capturing and collecting them without knowing what I was going to do with them.

I have always been painfully shy and interacting with the world is not easy, but this connects me with it and it’s how I can speak about it. Photography is a solitary practice and making work can be so isolating - I was scared to show my work, scared of being rejected or misunderstood, but I wanted to tell this story. People look at this book and think it’s bleak – and sure, it is, but there’s also a lot of hope in it. The last image of a cat, moving out of the frame to the right, is about moving forward and going on living, despite all of this.

How About Never is published by MACK.

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘It detonated right outside our house’: the explosion that started an incredible podcast series
EntertainmentTab.text:
In 2012, the US marine turned freelance foreign correspondent Austin Tice disappeared in Syria. If he’s still alive, he’ll be the second-longest detained journalist in the world. That, says Josh Baker (speaking to me from Wales), was the podcast he thought he was making: “We thought we were looking for a missing person, and what we fell into was almost like a Bourne novel, utterly extraordinary. A world of espionage, spies, dictatorship.”

It’s also a story of American exceptionalism – the way the US saw itself in relation to the rest of the world. Moreover, “I don’t mean this in a crass way,” Baker says, “but through Austin’s story, we also learn a lot about the last 14 years of the civil war in Syria. We really go inside the regime’s industrial complex of disappearance and torture. As episode two begins, Assad is gone, and we enter into these facilities.”

Ultimately, the hunt for the people who know the truth about Tice, and the hunt for those responsible for these atrocities, are one and the same. “A lot of my work for the last decade has involved intelligence and espionage and dealing with intelligence agencies, and I have never received so many leaks from so many different places as I have with Austin Tice – from every direction imaginable. It is absolutely extraordinary.”

This is Baker’s third series of I’m Not a Monster for the BBC. The first two – one about an American woman, Sam, who disappears into the Islamic State caliphate with her young children when her husband becomes a sniper, and the other one about Shamima Begum – are extraordinary pieces of journalism. But just as extraordinary is the backstory of how they came about.

Now 37, Baker started as a night editor on the foreign desk of the Times, and did “a little bit of reporting on the Serbian refugee crisis, and from the Middle East”. By the mid-10s, he was directing Battle for Iraq (a Guardian/PBS co-production), embedded with Iraqi special forces. “The story of the day was that the coalition forces were defeating Isis, were kicking their ass basically. And the reality was quite different.” He got caught in the centre of Mosul and by nightfall had been offered a place to stay by a family, explosions and fighting happening all around. A radio operator woke the team with a warning, “and I could hear shooting”, he remembers, “but without wanting to sound like a war bro, it was all going one way and it was all American weaponry. The sound is different when it’s Isis.”

What he didn’t hear until too late was a massive articulated lorry, trying to manoeuvre its way down the street to deliver a car bomb. “I know this bit because Isis, the bastards, were filming from a drone. It detonated right outside our house and I was buried in the collapsing building, and broke my back.”

As he was recovering in England after his evacuation, a source of his heard he’d been injured and got in touch. “He’s now almost like a friend, but a source like that always has an agenda,” Baker says. “He showed me a home video from inside Raqqa, which was then the Isis capital, of a young American boy called Matthew being forced to assemble a suicide bomb. This wasn’t a propaganda video, it was a home video.”

Matthew was Sam’s oldest son. “I was obviously in a mental state, having just walked out of something by the skin of my teeth. But I thought: ‘I’m gonna find this kid,’ which sounds incredibly idealistic, but seven months later, I did.”

The Begum season also came out of that suicide bombing – a Dutch IS bride had been in Mosul at the same time, and some years later privately messaged Baker on Twitter, saying she was in the same refugee camp as Shamima Begum and her children (all three of whom have now died). Baker was more than familiar with Begum’s story – he’d been working as assistant producer on Welcome to the Mosque and had been inside her east London mosque the day she and her school friends disappeared in 2015. But his new source was the start of an incredibly rich picture of what life was like for these girls and young women when they reached Syria – the deprivation, the violence, the forced marriage, the jeopardy.

Baker was also, after a long research trip to Turkey, able to piece together the role of Canadian intelligence in getting Begum across the border, an act which in itself (in my view) was cynical enough that it should solidify Begum’s case that she is more victim than terrorist. He plays down the credit for that exclusive – had it been an action of British intelligence, he says, he’d never have been able to prove it, “because of the tradecraft. Whereas if you look at some of the American or Canadian, or even some European agencies, the tradecraft doesn’t seem to be there in the same way.”

The Dutch woman was repatriated to the Netherlands, where she served some of her prison sentence, before it was overturned on the basis that she had been groomed and abused by her husband. “Tens of thousands of people from potentially as many as 100 nations were convinced to go to Isis,” Baker says. “They had a highly effective campaign. Which isn’t to say that someone who’s been with Isis isn’t a threat, but you will struggle to find a security expert who’ll say that our current strategy” – stripping people like Begum of statehood – “is making us safer.”

Baker and his colleagues received a large number of death threats after that documentary. It touched on everything: terrorism and foreign policy, who gets to be British and whose Britishness will always be conditional, how much transparency one can ever expect from one’s government. “By the end of that programme, it wasn’t really about Shamima any more.”

“In Britain, when people say they have an intelligence source, they often mean they’ve spoken to a press officer,” Baker says. “In America, and particularly in Washington, that world is much more accessible. You can meet intelligence officers or senior law enforcement at dinner parties or even in bars. And still, a great deal of what I’m told I either can’t stand up or I’m told I can’t use. I will say, though, that under the Trump administration, people have become much less inclined to speak.”

That access really shows in the Austin Tice podcast, which feels extremely close to the source, and urgent in a way that you wouldn’t think possible for a case that, 14 years on, one would expect to be cold. “Genuinely, our first mission was to try to get answers to Austin’s mum. But also, I really want people to care about what happened in Syria, because it’s obscene. Conservatively, 100,000 people have been disappeared. One of the reasons I left news is I got very tired of having to explain complex things in a matter-of-fact way. The privilege of doing this kind of narrative investigative journalism is that I can slow down and make you care about the people.”

I wonder whether Baker chose Tice’s story because he identified with him: a young guy in a war zone, playing stark odds and never knowing which, among myriad dangers, might be decisive. “No, what I identified with was his mother. I remember seeing her do a press conference, nine or 10 years into his disappearance, and thinking about my own mum. I’m from a single-parent household – we’re very close. I just thought, ‘Jesus Christ, what an awful existence to have.’”

He thinks he has emerged from this investigation with “a pretty decent idea about what may have happened to Austin. Whether or not we could ever be definitive about it is a different thing.”

GeneralTab.title: Police launch criminal investigation into Reform UK donations
GeneralTab.text:
The Metropolitan Police is carrying out a criminal investigation into Reform UK over allegations it broke foreign funding laws, following a broadcast by Channel 4 News last week.

An undercover reporter recorded two senior Reform aides apparently suggesting a way around electoral law to secure foreign party donations, one of which would have totalled £500,000.

The police investigation by the Met's Special Enquiry Team is being folded into an inquiry that has been under way into other donations to the party.

A Reform UK spokesman said the party "denies any wrongdoing and will fully cooperate with the investigation".

"We won't be commenting further while a live investigation is under way."

A Met spokesperson said it had received "a number of reports relating to donations and polling involving a political party", after the film by Channel 4 News and Verbatim Investigations was shown on Thursday evening.

In its statement, the Met Police said: "All allegations under investigation relate to potential offences under the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000."

"Detectives continue to liaise closely with the Electoral Commission and Crown Prosecution Service as enquiries progress."

The police spokesperson said detectives were seeking to obtain footage relating to the broadcast.

The film overshadowed the party's conference in Birmingham and led to the party losing two key figures - Dan Jukes, chief of staff to the leader Nigel Farage, and James Orr, head of policy.

In the news report, an undercover investigator posing as the son of an American donor is recorded raising a concern that his father wouldn't be able to directly donate to the party within the law.

Electoral law states that to be a permissible donor to a UK political party you must be a UK registered voter, or a company registered in the UK.

Jukes appears to suggest that the donation could be in the UK-based son's name, although the money would have come from his American father.

Elsewhere James Orr, the party's head of policy suggests that the father could pay for opinion polling to support one of Reform's campaigns.

Farage and Jukes were also filmed at a lunch in Clacton where it is suggested the US donor, who was being played by an actor, gives £500,000 to Reform through his son.

Farage told the BBC he "frankly wasn't listening" to the discussion about the potential donation. Channel 4 News have said the payment was never made.

He dismissed the comments made by his aide in the film as "loose pub talk including a couple of boasts that simply were not true".

Jukes has denied "any wrongdoing" and said he had "stepped back from politics in order to clear my name".

Last week, Orr told Sky News he would cooperate with the party's internal investigation "fully".

The Met had already been investigating whether payments to Reform in the weeks before the last election complied with donation laws.

The probe is examining donations given directly to the party by Fiona Cottrell, mother of longstanding Nigel Farage ally, George Cottrell.

It is also examining payments from a company controlled by Reform's deputy leader Richard Tice, which received £1m from Fiona Cottrell in June 2024.

A Verbatim Investigations spokesperson said: "Verbatim will cooperate with the police's investigation."

GeneralTab.title: Andy Burnham: National security can't come at expense of social security
GeneralTab.text:
Andy Burnham has said national security "can't come at the expense of social security", as he was challenged over funding for defence at Prime Minister's Questions.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch pressed Burnham over whether he would spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030 and how he would pay for this.

The PM said the government's commitment to defence was "absolute" and he would set a target date to reach the 3% figure in the spring.

Burnham said he would fund defence and get the welfare bill down in "the Labour way", by changing education, supporting young people and providing more mental health support.

The Conservatives seized on the comments, with a party spokesperson saying: "Britain heard it loud and clear today: Andy Burnham will not cut welfare to fund the defence of our country.

"The prime minister is prioritising the ballooning benefits bill over our national security. Shameful."

After PMQs, Burnham's team was at pains to stress his commitment that "national security is the most important duty of any government", and stressed the prime minister had been "consistent about getting the welfare bill down".

But they said that did not mean "crude cuts" that could "put people into crisis" by making them homeless and so creating higher costs elsewhere in the system to support them.

In the Commons session, Burnham repeated that the government would meet the Nato target of spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035, with a target date for hitting the 3% figure set out in the spending review in the spring.

The PM said he had appointed John Healey, who resigned as Sir Keir Starmer's defence secretary over the government's failure to commit to a 3% increase by 2030, "because of his strong commitment to the defence of this nation".

However, Badenoch hit back that 2035 was "a decade away" and "the threats are now".

She questioned whether Burnham was "unable" or "just unwilling" to meet the 2030 target.

In response, Burnham insisted: "This chancellor of all chancellors will be willing to provide that funding to our armed forces."

However, he rejected a Conservative plan to partly fund increased defence spending by saving at least £4bn through reforms to housing benefit.

"I don't think, myself, that taking £4bn out of housing benefit is going to get the right consensus around this issue because that would create levels of homelessness in this country... that we wouldn't have seen before, hundreds of thousands of children in temporary accommodation," he said.

"Yes, we do everything to support our national security, but it can't come at the expense of social security."

He added: "This side of the House will not be forced to choose between the two and we will set out a plan to get to 3.5% by 2035 at the spending review."

Badenoch said Burnham's comments were "unbelievable", adding: "We need to fund our defence, not spend all of our money on welfare."

Burnham insisted he would "bring the welfare budget down" by tackling the number of young people not in education, employment or training.

"That's the Labour way to get the welfare bill down," he said.

"That is the right way to fund defence."

Badenoch accused Burnham of being "continuity Keir".

"He's pretending that he's the change candidate. But the fact is, he's still failing to cut welfare," she said.

As prime minister, Sir Keir attempted to cut disability benefits but was forced to row back on the plans in the face of opposition from Labour MPs.

Cutting the welfare bill is a key part of Tory proposals for funding increased defence spending.

Spending on benefits has ballooned in recent years and is forecast to rise to £408.6bn in 2030/31, according to figures from the Department for Work and Pensions.

There is particular concern about the nearly one million young people in the UK who are not in education, employment or training – known as "Neets".

The government has asked former minister Alan Milburn to look into the issue and he is expected to publish his final recommendations for how to tackle the problem shortly.

GeneralTab.title: Learner drivers still forced to wait months to book tests
GeneralTab.text:
Learner drivers have to wait an average 20 weeks, or around five months, before booking a practical test, according to new figures, despite attempts to reduce delays.

The data from the Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency (DVSA) for August is only a marginal improvement from 20.2 weeks in July.

The average wait time between booking and sitting a test is unchanged at 11.1 weeks.

The DVSA initially had a target of reducing the average waiting time to seven weeks by the end of last year. Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander pushed the target back to summer 2026, but subsequently admitted even that would not be possible.

The DVSA made a number of changes to its practical driving test booking system earlier this year.

Only the learner driver themself is now able to book their driving test, blocking an instructor or third parties from booking using the learner's details.

There is also a geographical restriction which means a learner can only book a test at their three local test centres, rather than one at the other side of the country if they found a test available.

The number of times a would-be driver can swap a test date has also been restricted.

The DVSA said on Wednesday that more than 2.13 million practical driving tests took place in the 12 months to August 2026 – the highest rolling 12-month figure on record.

DVSA chief executive Beverley Warmington, said: "There's more to do and we're not going to stop until every learner can get a fair test slot when they need one but today's figures show our plan is working."

Carly Brookfield, the chief executive of the Driving Instructors Association, said the higher number of available tests was "progress that should be recognised" but, for learners and instructors "the pressure is still very real".

"The ultimate measure of recovery has to be a testing service that learners and the professional training community can access when they need it," she said.

Adem Veli, who has been an instructor for 16 years and runs his driving school Passman in Sidcup, said: "Before Covid we had the luxury we could pick the test date and work towards that date."

But he said learners having to wait so long can have a huge impact on their confidence.

"It's about a six month wait," he said. "Can you imagine if you did fail your driving test, you're test standard and ready to go [but] have to wait another six months to get back in?"

DVSA figures revealed that the pass rate for driving tests remains over 50%.

GeneralTab.title: What are my rights if my flight is cancelled or delayed?
GeneralTab.text:
Thousands of air passengers have seen their travel plans disrupted after an air traffic control problem grounded nearly 2,000 flights across the UK.

When a flight is cancelled or delayed, passengers affected have various rights – such as a refund or be put on another flight. However, these can vary depending on which carrier you are flying with and from where.

Only when an airline is at fault - not issues such as air traffic control problems - is extra compensation payable. Here's what it means for you.

When flights are delayed or cancelled, UK and EU airlines, and other carriers when you are departing a UK or EU airport, have a duty to look after you.

The reason for the delay or cancellation does not matter. So anyone affected by the air transport delays will be eligible.

That includes providing meals and accommodation, if necessary, and getting you to your destination. The airline should organise putting you on an alternative flight, at no extra cost.

Additional losses, such as unused accommodation, might require a claim to a credit card provider, if that was the payment option used.

After that, a claim may need to go to your travel insurance provider. But there is no standard definition of what is covered.

It may require a close look at the details of the policy to see what is covered, and in which circumstances.

Passengers are also being urged to heed travel advice from the UK government, external, as this can also affect travel insurance rights.

If your flight is covered by UK law, your airline must let you choose between either getting a refund or being booked on to an alternative flight.

That's regardless of how far in advance the cancellation was made.

You can get your money back for any part of the ticket you have not used.

So, if you booked a return flight and the outbound leg is cancelled, you can get the full cost of the return ticket refunded.

If you still want to travel, your airline must find you an alternative flight.

If another airline is flying to your destination significantly sooner, or there are other suitable modes of transport, then you have a right to be booked on to that alternative transport instead.

If your flight was coming into the UK on a non-UK or EU airline, then you should check the terms and conditions of your booking.

If you are stuck abroad or at the airport because of a flight cancellation, airlines covered by UK legislation must also provide you with other assistance.

a reasonable amount of food and drink (often in the form of vouchers)

a way for you to communicate (often by refunding the cost of calls)

free accommodation, if you have to stay overnight to fly the next day

transport to and from the accommodation

If your airline is unable to arrange assistance, you have the right to organise this yourself and claim back the cost later.

The Civil Aviation Authority advises people to keep receipts and not spend more than necessary.

You are entitled to the same assistance as for a cancellation if your flight is delayed by more than two hours for a short-haul flight, three hours for a medium-haul, or four hours for a long-haul.

If you are delayed by more than five hours and no longer want to travel, you can get a full refund.

Airlines will not refund you for loss of earnings. Travel insurance policies will not usually cover loss of earnings either.

If you think you're going to be late back at work because of flight delays, you have a responsibility to let your employer know, legal experts say.

You should agree with your employer how to deal with the absence – for example, by using annual leave or taking unpaid leave.

Employers have no legal obligation to pay employees who are absent in this situation, experts say, unless it is stated in their contract.

articles.title: Police launch criminal investigation into Reform UK donations
articles.text:
The Metropolitan Police is carrying out a criminal investigation into Reform UK over allegations it broke foreign funding laws, following a broadcast by Channel 4 News last week.

An undercover reporter recorded two senior Reform aides apparently suggesting a way around electoral law to secure foreign party donations, one of which would have totalled £500,000.

The police investigation by the Met's Special Enquiry Team is being folded into an inquiry that has been under way into other donations to the party.

A Reform UK spokesman said the party "denies any wrongdoing and will fully cooperate with the investigation".

"We won't be commenting further while a live investigation is under way."

A Met spokesperson said it had received "a number of reports relating to donations and polling involving a political party", after the film by Channel 4 News and Verbatim Investigations was shown on Thursday evening.

In its statement, the Met Police said: "All allegations under investigation relate to potential offences under the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000."

"Detectives continue to liaise closely with the Electoral Commission and Crown Prosecution Service as enquiries progress."

The police spokesperson said detectives were seeking to obtain footage relating to the broadcast.

The film overshadowed the party's conference in Birmingham and led to the party losing two key figures - Dan Jukes, chief of staff to the leader Nigel Farage, and James Orr, head of policy.

In the news report, an undercover investigator posing as the son of an American donor is recorded raising a concern that his father wouldn't be able to directly donate to the party within the law.

Electoral law states that to be a permissible donor to a UK political party you must be a UK registered voter, or a company registered in the UK.

Jukes appears to suggest that the donation could be in the UK-based son's name, although the money would have come from his American father.

Elsewhere James Orr, the party's head of policy suggests that the father could pay for opinion polling to support one of Reform's campaigns.

Farage and Jukes were also filmed at a lunch in Clacton where it is suggested the US donor, who was being played by an actor, gives £500,000 to Reform through his son.

Farage told the BBC he "frankly wasn't listening" to the discussion about the potential donation. Channel 4 News have said the payment was never made.

He dismissed the comments made by his aide in the film as "loose pub talk including a couple of boasts that simply were not true".

Jukes has denied "any wrongdoing" and said he had "stepped back from politics in order to clear my name".

Last week, Orr told Sky News he would cooperate with the party's internal investigation "fully".

The Met had already been investigating whether payments to Reform in the weeks before the last election complied with donation laws.

The probe is examining donations given directly to the party by Fiona Cottrell, mother of longstanding Nigel Farage ally, George Cottrell.

It is also examining payments from a company controlled by Reform's deputy leader Richard Tice, which received £1m from Fiona Cottrell in June 2024.

A Verbatim Investigations spokesperson said: "Verbatim will cooperate with the police's investigation."

articles.title: Andy Burnham: National security can't come at expense of social security
articles.text:
Andy Burnham has said national security "can't come at the expense of social security", as he was challenged over funding for defence at Prime Minister's Questions.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch pressed Burnham over whether he would spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030 and how he would pay for this.

The PM said the government's commitment to defence was "absolute" and he would set a target date to reach the 3% figure in the spring.

Burnham said he would fund defence and get the welfare bill down in "the Labour way", by changing education, supporting young people and providing more mental health support.

The Conservatives seized on the comments, with a party spokesperson saying: "Britain heard it loud and clear today: Andy Burnham will not cut welfare to fund the defence of our country.

"The prime minister is prioritising the ballooning benefits bill over our national security. Shameful."

After PMQs, Burnham's team was at pains to stress his commitment that "national security is the most important duty of any government", and stressed the prime minister had been "consistent about getting the welfare bill down".

But they said that did not mean "crude cuts" that could "put people into crisis" by making them homeless and so creating higher costs elsewhere in the system to support them.

In the Commons session, Burnham repeated that the government would meet the Nato target of spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035, with a target date for hitting the 3% figure set out in the spending review in the spring.

The PM said he had appointed John Healey, who resigned as Sir Keir Starmer's defence secretary over the government's failure to commit to a 3% increase by 2030, "because of his strong commitment to the defence of this nation".

However, Badenoch hit back that 2035 was "a decade away" and "the threats are now".

She questioned whether Burnham was "unable" or "just unwilling" to meet the 2030 target.

In response, Burnham insisted: "This chancellor of all chancellors will be willing to provide that funding to our armed forces."

However, he rejected a Conservative plan to partly fund increased defence spending by saving at least £4bn through reforms to housing benefit.

"I don't think, myself, that taking £4bn out of housing benefit is going to get the right consensus around this issue because that would create levels of homelessness in this country... that we wouldn't have seen before, hundreds of thousands of children in temporary accommodation," he said.

"Yes, we do everything to support our national security, but it can't come at the expense of social security."

He added: "This side of the House will not be forced to choose between the two and we will set out a plan to get to 3.5% by 2035 at the spending review."

Badenoch said Burnham's comments were "unbelievable", adding: "We need to fund our defence, not spend all of our money on welfare."

Burnham insisted he would "bring the welfare budget down" by tackling the number of young people not in education, employment or training.

"That's the Labour way to get the welfare bill down," he said.

"That is the right way to fund defence."

Badenoch accused Burnham of being "continuity Keir".

"He's pretending that he's the change candidate. But the fact is, he's still failing to cut welfare," she said.

As prime minister, Sir Keir attempted to cut disability benefits but was forced to row back on the plans in the face of opposition from Labour MPs.

Cutting the welfare bill is a key part of Tory proposals for funding increased defence spending.

Spending on benefits has ballooned in recent years and is forecast to rise to £408.6bn in 2030/31, according to figures from the Department for Work and Pensions.

There is particular concern about the nearly one million young people in the UK who are not in education, employment or training – known as "Neets".

The government has asked former minister Alan Milburn to look into the issue and he is expected to publish his final recommendations for how to tackle the problem shortly.

articles.title: Funeral for PC Matthew Blades killed in Middlesbrough A66 crash takes place
articles.text:
Hundreds have turned out for the funeral of one of the police officers killed in a wrong-way crash.

PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, died when a Volkswagen Passat collided with their marked armed response car on the A66 at South Bank, near Middlesbrough, on 22 August. Five young men were also killed.

A full ceremonial police funeral took place for PC Blades in Hartlepool earlier, with hundreds of officers from Cleveland and forces across the country lining the street in a guard of honour.

Speaking on behalf of his family, Cleveland Police Federation chair Lauren Somerville said "life feels unbearably quiet" without the father-of-two's "silly jokes" and laughter.

Members of other emergency services were present at St Joseph's Roman Catholic Church, alongside community leaders and politicians.

Cleveland Police chief constable Victoria Fuller greeted mourners at the entrance to the church.

Policing minister Sarah Jones and Home Office minister Anna Turley also attended.

The black hearse, led by a single Cleveland Police motorcycle, was surrounded by officers and bagpipe players.

On top was a simple floral display spelling out 'dad'.

Officers lowered their flags at the side of the street for the procession to pass while uniformed officers carried PC Blades' coffin, wrapped in a union flag, into the church as Amazing Grace was played by the pipers.

Members of the public also lined the streets to pay their respects.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham paid tribute in the Commons earlier, saying: "I also want to send our sympathies to the hundreds of people who will gather today at the funeral of PC Matthew Blades, including many serving police officers, and we send our thanks to them all for their service and their work to keep our community safe."

Somerville said flowers had been delivered to the force's stations and people from Australia, France and America had been in touch.

"The support has been overwhelming and it's been comforting," she said.

Somerville added even small acknowledgements of respect from the public, such as a nod or a thank you when they see police out and about, had brought officers "so much strength".

The force federation chair said Cleveland officers stood side-by-side in uniform at the funeral "filled with pride and dignity".

"I've spoken to Matthew's family and he was described as a best friend, a husband, a father, a brother and a son," Somerville said.

"He was funny and his laughter and silly jokes made them smile even when they least expected it, he brought light and laughter into every room he came into.

"And life feels unbearably quiet without him now."

PC Blades taught English at Carmel College in Darlington before joining the police force.

The school remembered him as an "intelligent, kind and approachable teacher" who "gave generously of himself to the young people in his care".

articles.title: Actor Noel Clarke charged with sexual offences
articles.text:
Actor Noel Clarke has been charged with sexual offences including sexual assault, voyeurism and exposure.

The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) authorised the Metropolitan Police to charge the Doctor Who and Kidulthood star on Wednesday.

Clarke, 50, from Kensington, west London, was charged with two counts of sexual assault, three charges of voyeurism and one charge of exposure. The offences are alleged to have taken place between 2007 and 2016 and relate to five women.

Clarke has not yet publicly responded to the charges.

In a statement released on Wednesday, the CPS said: "Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring this case to court and that it is in the public interest to do so."

The charges follow an investigation by detectives which began a year ago.

A man, then in his 40s, was first arrested in connection with the investigation on 25 September 2025.

A file of evidence was later given to the CPS who authorised charges.

Clarke will appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on 21 October at 10:00 BST.

Det Supt Mike Cagney, whose team is leading the investigation, said: "The women connected to these charges continue to receive support from specially trained officers.

"We urge anyone who has been a victim of sexual assault to contact police. The information you provide will be dealt with in the utmost sensitivity and we have trained investigators on hand to support you."

Clarke found fame playing Mickey Smith in Doctor Who between 2005 and 2010, and went on to become a successful actor, writer, producer and director.

articles.title: Germany's Merz attacks AfD in parliament after far-right election win
articles.text:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has clashed with AfD leader Alice Weidel in parliament, calling her party a "destructive force" with a migration policy that amounts to "ethnic cleansing" for skilled workers.

Merz was addressing the Bundestag in the aftermath of the anti-immigration party's sweeping victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt where it won almost 44% of the vote, while the chancellor's conservatives saw their vote halved.

Weidel told MPs that voters had shown that Merz's coalition with the centre left was a total failure and his time was up.

Merz hit back saying the AfD had harmed German interests by backing Russia, and its "remigration" policy would affect millions.

It is not yet clear whether the party will be able to form a government or not in Saxony-Anhalt, having fallen three seats short of an outright majority. No far-right party has won power in any of Germany's 16 states since World War Two, and Merz has admitted the "seismic" result has changed Germany.

The AfD's success has been praised by US President Donald Trump, who said "the Populist Party in Germany just had a really big night", linking the victory to "absolutely horrible immigration rules and regulations".

The AfD in Saxony-Anhalt has been labelled as "right-wing extremist" by German domestic intelligence and the party has promised a "deportation and remigration" offensive targeting irregular migrants.

Trump had been due to speak by phone to the German chancellor on Wednesday to mark the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks in the US, but the government spokesman in Berlin said the call had been postponed without saying why. No new date has been set.

Repeatedly heckled by AfD MPs, the chancellor told Weidel that one in six skilled workers had a migration background, and if her party had its way then its policy would amount to "nothing other than an ethnic cleansing in the skilled trades based on skin colour and origin".

While the government understood some deportations were needed, he said it made a careful distinction between those who contributed to German prosperity and those without permanent residency.

Disruption by AfD MPs became so loud that at one point Bundestag President Julia Klöckner threatened to start expelling people from the chamber: "We are not on a football pitch."

Weidel said mass migration had left Germans with daily knife violence and attacks on trains and in stations, but Merz warned that the AfD's plans would mean that no single care home, hospital or restaurant could function.
